title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
summary: How the six simple machines, such as the lever, pulley, and ramp, make work easier by trading less force for a longer distance.
poll: Machines make work easier without any cost at all.

versions.title: Tools That Help
versions.text:
Do you need to lift a big box? Push it, pull it, or lift it. That is work. A machine can make work less hard.

Some machines are not big. They have few parts. We call them simple machines. There are six kinds.

A lever is a bar. It rests on a point. Think of a seesaw. Push down on one end. The other end goes up. Put the point near the load. Then you need less force.

A pulley is a rope on a wheel. Pull the rope down. The load goes up. A flag goes up a pole this way.

A ramp is a slope. You push a load up it. That takes less force than a lift. But the path is long.

A wedge splits things. An axe is a wedge. A screw is a ramp that winds round a post. A wheel and axle turns, like a doorknob.

So a machine gives you a help. You use less force. But you must push it a long way. A bike has lots of these parts in one.

versions.text:
Have you tried to lift a big box? You push, pull, or lift it. That is work. A machine can make work feel less hard.

Not all machines are big. Some have just one or two parts. We call them simple machines. There are six kinds of them.

A lever is a long bar that rests on a point. A seesaw is a lever. When you push one end down, the other end goes up. If the point is near the load, you need less force.

A pulley is a rope that goes over a wheel. You pull the rope down, and the load goes up. This is how a flag goes up a pole. It is how a bucket comes up from a well.

A ramp is a slope. It is less hard to push a box up a ramp than to lift it. But the path is long.

A wedge, like an axe, splits things. A screw is a ramp that winds round a post. A wheel and axle, like a doorknob, turns.

Here is the deal. A machine lets you use less force. But you must move a long way. A bike puts lots of these parts in one.

versions.title: Simple Machines Help Us
versions.text:
Have you ever tried to lift a heavy box? When you push, pull, or lift something, you are doing work. A machine is a tool that makes work easier.

Not all machines have motors. Some have only one or two parts. These are called simple machines. There are six kinds: the lever, the pulley, the ramp, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a stiff bar that rests on a point. A seesaw is a lever. When you push one end down, the other end goes up. If you move the point close to the load, you need less force to lift it.

A pulley is a rope that goes over a wheel. When you pull the rope down, the load goes up. A flag is raised this way. In old villages, a bucket of water was pulled up from a well with a pulley.

A ramp is a flat slope. It is easier to push a heavy box up a ramp than to lift it straight up. But the path is longer.

A wedge, like an axe or a knife, splits things apart. A screw is a ramp that winds around a post, like the lid of a jar. A wheel and axle, like a doorknob, turns a small rod with a big wheel.

Here is the secret. A machine lets you use less force, but you must move a longer way. A bike and a pair of scissors join simple machines together.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Have you ever tried to lift a heavy box of books? Whenever you push, pull, or lift something, scientists say you are doing work. A machine is any tool that makes this work easier.

Many machines have engines and lots of moving parts. But some machines are very simple, with only one or two parts. These are called simple machines. There are six kinds: the lever, the pulley, the ramp, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a stiff bar that rests on a turning point. A seesaw is a good example. When you push one end down, the other end rises. If you move the turning point closer to the load, you need less force to lift it.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a wheel. When you pull down on the rope, the load moves up. This is how a flag is raised on a pole. In old villages, people used a pulley to raise buckets of water from deep wells.

A ramp is a flat, sloping surface. Pushing a heavy cart up a ramp takes much less force than lifting it straight up. However, the path along the ramp is longer.

A wedge, such as an axe or a knife, splits things apart. A screw is really a ramp that wraps around a post, like the lid of a jar. A wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a big wheel to turn a small rod.

There is always a trade. A machine lets you use less force, but you must move it over a longer distance. Bicycles and scissors combine several simple machines.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine trying to lift a heavy box of books onto a high shelf. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it moves, scientists say you are doing work. A machine is any device that makes this work easier for people.

Many machines, such as cars and washing machines, have engines and hundreds of moving parts. Some machines, however, are so basic that they have only one or two parts. These are called simple machines, and there are six main types: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a stiff bar that turns on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar example. When you push one end down, the other end rises. If you move the fulcrum closer to the load, you need less effort to lift it.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. When you pull down on the rope, the load moves up. Pulleys raise flags on poles, and in old villages they helped people lift buckets of water from deep wells.

An inclined plane is a ramp. Pushing a heavy cart up a ramp takes much less effort than lifting it straight up, but the path is longer.

A wedge, such as an axe, splits things apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a post, like the lid of a jar. A wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a large wheel to turn a small rod called an axle.

Every machine involves a trade. You use less effort, but you must move over a longer distance. Bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine trying to lift a heavy carton of books onto a high shelf. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it moves, scientists say that you are doing work. A machine is any device that makes this work easier by changing how much force you need or which direction you push.

Many machines, such as cars and washing machines, contain engines and hundreds of moving parts. Others, however, are so basic that they have only one or two parts. These are known as simple machines, and there are six main types: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar example: when one end goes down, the other end rises. If you move the fulcrum closer to the load, you need less effort to raise it.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. Pulling down on the rope lifts the load upward, which is often easier than lifting it directly. Pulleys raise flags on poles, and in traditional villages they helped people lift buckets of water from deep wells.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a heavy cart up a ramp requires far less effort than lifting it vertically, although the path is longer.

A wedge, such as an axe, splits materials apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a post, like the lid of a jar. A wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a large wheel to rotate a smaller rod called an axle.

Every machine involves a trade. You apply less effort, but you must move over a greater distance. Bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines.

Many modern machines, such as automobiles and washing machines, contain powerful engines and hundreds of interacting parts. These are known as simple machines, and scientists generally identify six main types: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar example, because one end rises whenever the other end is pushed down. If you position the fulcrum closer to the load, you need considerably less effort to raise it.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a loaded cart up a ramp requires far less effort than lifting it vertically, although the cart must travel a considerably longer path.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine attempting to lift a heavy carton of books onto a high shelf without any assistance. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it actually moves, scientists say that you are doing work, and a machine is any device that makes this work easier, either by reducing the force you must exert or by changing the direction in which you apply it.

Many modern machines, such as automobiles and washing machines, contain powerful engines and hundreds of interacting parts. Others, however, are so fundamental that they consist of only one or two components. These are known as simple machines, and scientists generally identify six main types: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar example, since one end rises whenever the other end is pushed down. If you position the fulcrum closer to the load, you need considerably less effort to raise it, and engineers call this benefit mechanical advantage.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. Pulling downward on the rope lifts the load upward, which is often more comfortable than lifting it directly, and in traditional villages pulleys helped families haul heavy buckets of water from deep wells.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a loaded cart up a ramp requires far less effort than lifting it vertically, although the cart must travel a considerably longer path to reach the same height.

A wedge, such as an axe, separates materials by forcing them apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a central post, and the spiral ridges of a jar lid, called threads, work in exactly this way. A wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a large wheel to rotate a smaller rod called an axle.

Every machine involves an exchange, because you exert less force but must move over a greater distance, so the total work never becomes smaller. In fact, real machines always lose a little energy to friction, the rubbing that slows moving parts. Bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines into a single useful device.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine attempting to lift a heavy carton of books onto a high shelf without any assistance. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it actually moves, physicists say that you are doing work, and a machine is any device that makes this work easier, either by reducing the force you must exert or by changing the direction in which you apply it.

Many modern machines, such as automobiles and washing machines, contain powerful engines and hundreds of interacting components, whereas others are so fundamental that they consist of only one or two parts. These are known as simple machines, and scientists traditionally identify six categories: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar example, since one end rises whenever the other end is pushed down. If you position the fulcrum closer to the load, you need considerably less effort to raise it, and engineers describe this benefit as mechanical advantage, a measure of how much a machine multiplies your force.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. Pulling downward on the rope lifts the load upward, which is often more comfortable than lifting it directly, and in traditional villages pulleys helped families haul heavy buckets of water from remarkably deep wells.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a loaded cart up a ramp requires substantially less effort than lifting it vertically, although the cart must travel a considerably longer path to reach the identical height.

A wedge, such as an axe, separates materials by forcing them apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a central post, and the spiral ridges of a jar lid, called threads, operate in precisely this way. A wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a large wheel to rotate a smaller rod called an axle.

Every machine involves an exchange, because you exert less force but must move over a greater distance, so the total work never becomes smaller. In reality, machines always lose a little energy to friction, the rubbing that slows moving surfaces, and bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines into a single, remarkably useful device.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine attempting to lift a heavy carton of books onto a high shelf without any assistance whatsoever. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it actually moves, physicists say that you are performing work, and a machine is any device that makes this work easier, either by reducing the force you must exert or by altering the direction in which you apply it.

Many contemporary machines, such as automobiles and washing machines, contain powerful engines and hundreds of interacting components, whereas others are so fundamental that they consist of merely one or two parts. These devices are known as simple machines, and scientists traditionally identify six categories: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle, each of which appears in countless everyday objects.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fixed point called a fulcrum. A seesaw is a familiar illustration, since one end rises whenever the other end is pushed down. If you position the fulcrum closer to the load, you need considerably less effort to elevate it, and engineers describe this benefit as mechanical advantage, a measurement of how effectively a machine multiplies the force you apply.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. Pulling downward on the rope lifts the load upward, which is frequently more comfortable than lifting it directly. In traditional villages, pulleys enabled families to haul heavy buckets of water from remarkably deep wells, and similar arrangements still raise flags and construction materials today.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a loaded cart up a ramp requires substantially less effort than lifting it vertically, although the cart must travel a considerably longer path to reach the identical elevation.

A wedge, such as an axe, separates materials by forcing them apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a central cylinder, and the spiral ridges of a jar lid, called threads, operate in precisely this manner, while a wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a large wheel to rotate a narrower rod called an axle.

Every machine involves an exchange, because you exert less force but must move across a greater distance, so the total work never actually decreases. In reality, machines always lose a little energy to friction, the resistance that develops whenever surfaces rub together, and bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines into a single, remarkably practical device.

versions.title: Simple Machines Make Work Easier
versions.text:
Imagine attempting to lift a heavy carton of encyclopedias onto an elevated shelf without any assistance whatsoever. Whenever you push, pull, or lift an object and it genuinely moves, physicists say that you are performing work, and a machine is any device that makes this work easier, either by reducing the force you must exert or by altering the direction in which you apply it.

Many contemporary machines, such as automobiles and washing machines, contain powerful engines and hundreds of interacting components, whereas others, however, are so fundamental that they consist of merely one or two parts. These devices are known as simple machines, and scientists traditionally identify six categories: the lever, the pulley, the inclined plane, the wedge, the screw, and the wheel and axle, each of which appears, often unnoticed, in countless everyday objects.

A lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a stationary point called a fulcrum, and a seesaw is a familiar illustration, since one end rises whenever the opposite end is pushed down. If you position the fulcrum closer to the load, you need considerably less effort to elevate it, and engineers describe this benefit as mechanical advantage, a measurement of how effectively a particular machine multiplies the force you apply.

A pulley is a rope that runs over a grooved wheel. Pulling downward on the rope lifts the load upward, which is frequently more comfortable than lifting it directly. In traditional villages, pulleys enabled families to haul heavy buckets of water from remarkably deep wells, and comparable arrangements still raise flags, elevators, and construction materials today.

An inclined plane is simply a ramp. Pushing a loaded cart up an inclined surface requires substantially less effort than lifting it vertically, although the cart must travel a considerably longer path to reach the identical elevation.

A wedge, such as an axe, separates materials by forcing them apart. A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a central cylinder, and the spiral ridges of a jar lid, called threads, operate in precisely this manner, while a wheel and axle, such as a doorknob, uses a comparatively large wheel to rotate a narrower rod called an axle.

Every machine involves an exchange, because you exert less force but must move across a greater distance, so the total work never actually decreases. In reality, machines invariably lose a little energy to friction, the resistance that develops whenever surfaces rub against each other, and bicycles and scissors are compound machines, which combine several simple machines into a single, remarkably practical device.

keyWords.definition: a tool or device that helps people do work
keyWords.example: My grandmother uses a sewing machine to make dresses.
Ali used a lot of force to open the stuck window.

keyWords.definition: a bar that rests on one point and helps lift or move things
keyWords.example: Dad used a long metal lever to lift the heavy rock.

keyWords.definition: a wheel with a rope over it that helps lift things
keyWords.example: The workers raised the bricks to the roof with a pulley.

keyWords.definition: a slope that joins a low place to a high place
keyWords.example: Sara rolled her bike up the ramp to the front door.

questions.stem: What is this article mostly about?
options: How to build a new bicycle
How simple machines make work easier
Why people should never lift boxes
How flags are made
questions.why: The article tells about the six simple machines and how each one makes work easier.

wrong.A: A bike is named at the end, but the article does not tell how to build one.
wrong.C: The article does not say people should never lift boxes.
wrong.D: A flag is one example of a pulley. The article is not about making flags.

questions.stem: What is a lever?
options: A rope that goes over a wheel
A thin edge that splits wood
A bar that rests on a point
A slope that goes up
questions.why: The article says a lever is a bar that rests on a point, like a seesaw.

wrong.A: A rope over a wheel is a pulley.
wrong.B: A thin edge that splits things is a wedge.
wrong.D: A slope is a ramp.

questions.stem: When you pull a pulley rope down, what happens to the load?
options: It goes up.
It falls off.
It gets heavier.
It stays still.
questions.why: The article says you pull the rope down and the load goes up, like a flag going up a pole.

wrong.B: The article does not say the load falls off.
wrong.C: The pulley does not change how heavy the load is.
wrong.D: The load moves up. It does not stay still.

questions.stem: Which tool is a wedge?
options: A doorknob
A seesaw
A flag pole
An axe
questions.why: The article says an axe is a wedge that splits things.

wrong.A: A doorknob is a wheel and axle.
wrong.C: A flag pole uses a pulley.

questions.stem: Read: "You use less force." What does force mean here?
options: A kind of rope
A push or a pull
A long path
A group of tools
questions.why: Force is the push or pull you use to move something. The article says a machine lets you use less of it.

wrong.A: A rope is part of a pulley, not a force.
wrong.C: The long path is the distance you move, not the force.
wrong.D: Force does not mean a group of tools.

questions.stem: Why might a worker push a heavy box up a ramp instead of lifting it?
options: Because the ramp makes the box smaller
Because the ramp moves the box by itself
Because the ramp takes less force
Because the ramp is a short path
questions.why: The article says a ramp takes less force than lifting, so the worker does not need to push as hard.

wrong.A: A ramp does not change the size of the box.
wrong.B: The worker still has to push. The ramp does not move it alone.
wrong.D: The article says the path on a ramp is long, not short.

questions.stem: The article says a machine lets you use less force. What is the cost?
options: You must move a longer way.
You must use two hands.
You must work at night.
You must pay for the machine.
questions.why: The article says you use less force, but you must move farther. That is the trade.

wrong.B: The article does not talk about using two hands.
wrong.D: The article does not talk about money.

questions.stem: How does the author explain each simple machine?
options: By telling a story about one farmer
By giving each machine and an everyday example of it
By listing the machines from newest to oldest
By comparing machines in a chart
questions.why: The author names each machine and gives a thing we know, like a seesaw, a flag, an axe, or a doorknob.

wrong.A: There is no story about a farmer.
wrong.C: The article does not say which machines are newer or older.
wrong.D: There is no chart in the article.

LOW.prompt: Pick one simple machine from the article. Tell what it does and name a place you have seen one.
checklist: I told how it makes work easier.
I gave a real example from my life.
LOW.modelAnswer: I will pick the lever. A lever is a simple machine that uses less force to lift something heavy. I have seen a lever used on a seesaw at the playground, where pushing down on one end lifts the other end up. A ramp and a pulley work in a similar way, by making it easier to move something without using as much force.

keyWords.definition: the point that a lever turns on
keyWords.example: The rock under the stick worked as a fulcrum.

keyWords.definition: the force or hard work you put into doing something
keyWords.example: It took a lot of effort to carry the water jugs upstairs.

keyWords.definition: sloping up or down, not flat
keyWords.example: The inclined path made the walk to the hilltop easier.

keyWords.definition: a piece with a thin edge that pushes things apart
keyWords.example: Mona slid a rubber wedge under the door to keep it open.

keyWords.definition: a rod in the middle of a wheel that turns with it
keyWords.example: The cart stopped when its axle broke.

questions.stem: Which sentence best states the central idea of the article?
options: Simple machines are too old to be useful today.
Only machines with engines can do real work.
The six simple machines make work easier by changing how we use force.
A seesaw is the most important machine ever made.
questions.why: The article explains six simple machines and how each makes work easier by changing the force or its direction.

wrong.A: The article shows simple machines in things we use today, like doorknobs and bicycles.
wrong.B: The article says simple machines with one or two parts also make work easier.
wrong.D: A seesaw is only one example of a lever.

questions.stem: According to the article, what is a fulcrum?
options: The fixed point a lever turns on
The rope in a pulley
The sharp edge of a wedge
The rod in the center of a wheel
questions.why: The article says a lever turns on a fixed point called a fulcrum.

wrong.B: A pulley uses a rope, but that is not a fulcrum.
wrong.C: The edge of a wedge is not called a fulcrum.
wrong.D: The rod in a wheel is the axle.

questions.stem: What does a screw have in common with an inclined plane?
options: Both use a rope that runs over a grooved wheel.
A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a post.
Both pivot on a fixed point called a fulcrum.
Neither one makes work any easier for people.
questions.why: The article says a screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a post, like a jar lid.

wrong.A: A rope and wheel make a pulley.
wrong.C: Levers pivot on a fulcrum, not screws or ramps.
wrong.D: The article says all simple machines make work easier.

questions.stem: A boy wants to lift a heavy rock with a long bar. Based on the article, what should he do?
options: Move the fulcrum farther from the rock
Use a shorter bar
Move the fulcrum closer to the rock
Push up on the bar instead of down
questions.why: The article says that moving the fulcrum closer to the load means you need less effort.

wrong.A: Moving the fulcrum away from the load would make it harder.
wrong.B: The article does not say a shorter bar helps.
wrong.D: With a seesaw-type lever, you push one end down to raise the other.

questions.stem: Read: "An inclined plane is a ramp." What does inclined mean?
options: Sloping
Heavy
Round
Sharp
questions.why: An inclined plane is a ramp, a surface that slopes up from a low place to a high place.

wrong.B: Heavy describes a load, not the shape of a ramp.
wrong.C: A wheel is round. A ramp is a flat slope.
wrong.D: A wedge has a sharp edge, but a ramp is not sharp.

questions.stem: Why does the author say that every machine involves a trade?
options: Because machines must be bought in shops for money
Because you use less effort but move a longer distance
Because most machines break after only a few uses
Because people often trade their machines with each other
questions.why: The article explains that a machine lowers the effort you need, but you must move farther to do the job.

wrong.A: Buying is not the kind of trade the article means.
wrong.C: The article does not say machines break quickly.
wrong.D: The article is not about swapping machines.

questions.stem: Why does the author mention buckets being raised from wells in old villages?
options: To show that pulleys have helped people for a long time
To explain how wells are dug
To prove that ramps are better than pulleys
To describe what villages looked like
questions.why: The example shows a real, long-standing use of the pulley in people's daily lives.

wrong.B: The article does not explain digging wells.
wrong.C: The example is about pulleys only and does not compare them to ramps.
wrong.D: The article does not describe what villages looked like.

questions.stem: Why are bicycles and scissors called compound machines?
options: They have small engines inside them.
They are made of strong metal parts.
They are used only by grown-up adults.
They join several simple machines.
questions.why: The article says compound machines combine several simple machines.

wrong.A: Bicycles and scissors do not have engines.
wrong.B: What they are made of is not why they are compound.
wrong.C: The article never says who uses them.

MID.prompt: Explain how a lever or an inclined plane makes work easier. Use the words effort and distance in your answer.
checklist: I explained how the machine works.
I used the words effort and distance correctly.
I included one detail from the article.
MID.modelAnswer: A lever makes work easier by letting a person use less effort to lift a heavy load. The lever is a rigid bar that pivots on a fulcrum, and if you move the fulcrum closer to the load, you need even less effort to lift it, although your hand has to move over a longer distance to do so. An inclined plane, like a ramp, works in a similar way, because pushing a heavy object up a gentle ramp takes less effort than lifting it straight up, even though the object travels a greater distance along the slope. In the article, this trade between effort and distance is also what makes a wedge or an axle useful for making different kinds of work easier.

keyWords.definition: to use force or strength to do something

keyWords.example: "Sunflower" is a compound word made from two smaller words.

HIGH.prompt: Explain why the article says machines involve an exchange. Use an example from the text and mention the role of friction.
checklist: I explained the trade between force and distance.
I used at least one example from the article.
I described how friction affects real machines.
HIGH.modelAnswer: The article says machines involve an exchange because every simple machine trades the amount of force a person must exert for the distance over which that force is applied, rather than eliminating the work itself. For example, pushing a heavy cart up a ramp lets a person exert far less effort than lifting it straight up, but the advantage comes at the cost of moving the cart over a much longer distance along the slope. A screw, which is really an inclined plane wrapped around a thread, shows this exchange even more clearly, since turning it many times trades distance for the force needed to drive it into a surface. However, friction always works against this exchange in real machines, quietly resisting motion and wasting some of the effort as heat, which is why compound machines combining several simple machines, like bicycles, are carefully designed to keep friction as low as possible.
